usage: 흰 is the modifier form of 희다 placed before the noun
the shirt is a bit big
subject marker 가; 좀 softens the complaint
clothing is counted with 벌, never 개
examples: 셔츠를 입어요.
I wear a shirt.
Bare basics: the verb for putting on body clothing is 입다.
이 셔츠가 저한테 잘 맞아요.
This shirt fits me well.
잘 맞다 = to fit; the size partner-verb is 맞다, not 좋다.
면접 때문에 깔끔한 셔츠 한 벌 샀어요.
I bought one neat shirt for the interview.
Real situation: 깔끔하다 (neat/crisp) is the go-to adjective for dress shirts.
nuance: 셔츠 is the loanword for a collared upper-body shirt; the general Sino-Korean cover term for any top is 상의 (上衣, 'upper garment'), and a knit pullover is 티셔츠/티. Because a shirt covers the torso it ALWAYS takes 입다 ('put on the body'), the same family of dressing verbs that splits by body zone in Korean: 입다 for trunk and legs, 신다 for feet, 쓰다 for the head/face, 끼다 for hands. The single biggest English-speaker pitfall is treating 'wear' as one verb the way English does — you cannot say 셔츠를 써요 or 셔츠를 신어요. Register is neutral and the word fits any politeness level. Natural collocations: 셔츠를 입다/벗다 (put on/take off), 셔츠를 다리다 (iron a shirt), 셔츠가 (안) 맞다 (it does (not) fit). Note that to take a shirt off you switch to 벗다, not a negated 입다.

usage: legs are body clothing, so 입다 (not 신다)
긴 is the adnominal form of 길다 before a noun
subject marker 가; 바지 stays singular
counted with 벌, and treated as one item
examples: 바지를 입어요.
I wear pants.
Even though English is plural, 바지 is grammatically singular in Korean.
이 바지가 저한테 너무 길어요.
These pants are too long for me.
-한테 marks the person a measurement is judged against ('for me').
수선집에서 바지 길이를 줄였어요.
I had the pants shortened at the tailor's.
Real situation: 길이를 줄이다 (shorten the length) is the standard alteration phrase.
nuance: 바지 covers the lower body, so despite English treating 'pants' as plural, Korean treats it as a single uncountable garment: there is no plural ending, no 'a pair' built into the word, and the verb is 입다 just like a shirt. The dividing line with footwear matters — legs use 입다 but the feet that stick out below use 신다, so you 입다 your 바지 but 신다 your 양말. Jeans are 청바지 (靑—, 'blue-color pants'), shorts are 반바지 ('half pants'), and dress slacks are often just called 슬랙스. The classic English-speaker error is the literal plural reflex — saying 바지들이 길어요 sounds as odd as saying 'pantses'. Natural collocations: 바지를 입다/벗다, 바지를 갈아입다 (change into other pants), 바지 길이를 줄이다 (shorten), 바지가 끼다 (the pants are tight). Note 끼다 here means 'feel tight', a different sense from putting gloves on.

usage: 짧은 is the adnominal of 짧다 before the noun
어울리다 = to look good on someone
counted with the clothing counter 벌
examples: 치마를 입어요.
I wear a skirt.
Skirts use 입다, exactly like pants — both are lower-body garments.
이 치마가 좀 짧지 않아요?
Isn't this skirt a bit short?
-지 않아요? turns it into a soft, seeking-agreement question.
결혼식에 갈 거라서 단정한 치마를 골랐어요.
I picked a tidy skirt because I'm going to a wedding.
Real situation: 단정하다 (tidy/proper) is the register word for formal dressing; 고르다 = to pick.
nuance: 치마 is the native Korean word for a skirt and is purely neutral; the English loanword 스커트 exists but 치마 is what people actually say in daily life, and a traditional hanbok skirt is also 치마. Like all lower-body clothing it takes 입다, and to take it off you switch to 벗다 — never a negated 입다. The trap for English speakers is again the one-word-'wear' habit plus assuming a fancier loanword is more polite; here the plain native 치마 is the unmarked, fully appropriate choice in every register. A very useful partner verb is 어울리다 ('to suit/match'), used with the marker -이/가 for the item and -에게/한테 for the person: 그 치마가 너한테 잘 어울려. Natural collocations: 치마를 입다/벗다, 짧은/긴 치마 (short/long skirt), 치마가 어울리다, 치마를 갈아입다. Do not confuse 어울리다 (looks good on) with 맞다 (fits in size) — a skirt can 맞다 yet not 어울리다.

usage: outerwear is still body clothing, so 입다
두꺼운 is the adnominal of 두껍다 (ㅂ-irregular)
subject marker 가; 따뜻하다 describes warmth
counted with 벌 like other clothing
examples: 코트를 입어요.
I wear a coat.
An overcoat is worn on the body, so the verb is 입다, same as a shirt.
밖이 추우니까 코트를 입고 나가세요.
Since it's cold outside, put your coat on and go out.
-고 links 'put on' then 'go'; the sequence verb 입고 means 'having put on'.
올겨울에 입을 따뜻한 코트를 하나 장만했어요.
I got myself one warm coat to wear this winter.
Real situation: 장만하다 (acquire/get for oneself) is warmer and more natural than 사다 for a planned purchase.
nuance: 코트 is a loanword for a warm outer layer; the broader native umbrella term for any outerwear is 외투 (外套, 'outer wrap'), and a padded winter jacket is 패딩 or 점퍼. Even though it is the outermost layer, 코트 still takes 입다 because the rule keys off the body zone (trunk), not how many layers are underneath; you put it on with 입다 and take it off with 벗다. The English-speaker pitfall is pronunciation-driven spelling and the 'wear' reflex: 코트 is two clean syllables (ko-teu) and is never said with 쓰다 or 차다. A second subtlety: when you mean 'put a coat ON over other clothes' Koreans often say 코트를 걸치다 ('throw on lightly'), a nuance 입다 alone doesn't carry. Natural collocations: 코트를 입다/벗다, 코트를 걸치다 (drape on), 두꺼운/긴 코트, 코트 단추를 잠그다 (button up the coat). Note 걸치다 implies a casual, partial wearing, unlike the full 입다.

usage: head items take 쓰다, not 입다
빨간 is the adnominal of 빨갛다 (ㅎ-irregular)
어울리다 with the item marked by 가
accessories are commonly counted with 개/하나
examples: 모자를 써요.
I wear a hat.
Anything on the head uses 쓰다 — the same verb as for glasses.
햇볕이 강하니까 모자를 쓰는 게 좋아요.
Since the sun is strong, it's good to wear a hat.
쓰는 게 좋다 = 'it's good to wear', a gentle suggestion pattern.
야구장에서 응원하려고 팀 모자를 하나 샀어요.
I bought a team cap to cheer at the ballpark.
Real situation: 모자 covers both dress hats and baseball caps; context decides which.

The crucial verb is 쓰다 ('place on the head'), which Korean also uses for glasses and umbrellas; it does NOT take 입다. The headline English-speaker pitfall is twofold: the 'wear = 입다' overgeneralization, and the fact that 쓰다 is a notorious homonym — the same 쓰다 means 'to write' and 'to use' and even 'bitter'. So 모자를 써요 ('I wear a hat') and 편지를 써요 ('I write a letter') share a verb; only the object tells them apart. To take a hat off you use 벗다, the same removal verb as for body clothing. Natural collocations: 모자를 쓰다/벗다, 모자를 푹 눌러쓰다 (pull a cap down low), 모자가 어울리다, 모자를 거꾸로 쓰다 (wear a cap backwards). Note 눌러쓰다 fuses 누르다+쓰다 for jamming a cap down.

usage: anything on the feet takes 신다
두꺼운 is the adnominal of 두껍다 (ㅂ-irregular)
subject marker 이 after a consonant
paired footwear uses 켤레, not 벌
examples: 양말을 신어요.
I wear socks.
Feet take 신다 — the same verb as shoes, never 입다.
발이 시려서 두꺼운 양말을 신었어요.
My feet were cold so I put on thick socks.
발이 시리다 ('feet feel cold') is the idiomatic way to say cold feet.
편의점에서 양말 한 켤레만 사 신었어요.
I just bought and put on a pair of socks at the convenience store.
Real situation: 사 신다 (buy-and-wear) compounds the purchase with immediate use.
nuance: 양말 (洋襪, literally 'Western foot-wrap' — coined when Western-style knitted socks arrived) goes on the feet, so it takes 신다, the dedicated foot-dressing verb shared with shoes; it never takes 입다. Crucially it is counted with 켤레, the counter for things that come in matched pairs (also used for shoes and gloves), so 'one pair of socks' is 양말 한 켤레, and the English-speaker who reaches for 벌 (clothing) or 개 (generic) will sound off. The 'wear = one verb' habit is again the core trap: feet are their own zone in Korean's dressing system. A second pitfall is the subject particle — after the final consonant ㄹ you need 이, giving 양말이, not 양말가. Natural collocations: 양말을 신다/벗다, 양말 한 켤레, 발목 양말 (ankle socks), 양말에 구멍이 나다 (a hole forms in the sock). Note removal is again 벗다, and 구멍이 나다 ('a hole appears') uses 나다, not 생기다, in this fixed phrase.

usage: 따뜻한 is the adnominal of 따뜻하다
subject marker 이 after the consonant
examples: 장갑을 껴요.
I wear gloves.
Gloves slide onto the hands, so the natural verb is 끼다 (also said 끼우다).
손이 시려서 장갑을 끼고 나왔어요.
My hands were cold so I came out wearing gloves.
-고 chains 'put on' + 'come out'; 끼고 = 'having put on'.
설거지할 때 고무장갑을 껴요.
I wear rubber gloves when doing the dishes.
Real situation: 고무장갑 (rubber gloves) are a kitchen staple; 끼다 still applies.
nuance: 장갑 (掌匣, 'palm case' — 掌 'palm' + 匣 'small box/case') goes on the hands, and the most idiomatic verb is 끼다 ('to insert/slip into a snug space'), the same verb used for rings; you may also hear 끼우다 or the broad 하다, but 신다 and 입다 are wrong. This is the clearest demonstration that Korean dressing verbs are organized by body part, not by a single 'wear': hands have their own verb just as feet (신다) and head (쓰다) do. Like socks and shoes, gloves are counted in pairs with 켤레. The double English-speaker pitfall: defaulting to 입다, and forgetting that 끼다 also means 'to be stuck/jammed' or 'fog rolls in' (안개가 끼다), so context disambiguates. Natural collocations: 장갑을 끼다/벗다, 장갑 한 켤레, 고무장갑 (rubber gloves), 가죽 장갑 (leather gloves). Note that to remove gloves you again use 벗다, the universal Korean 'take off' verb.

usage: the catch-all verb 하다 works for a scarf
긴 is the adnominal of 길다 (ㄹ drops before ㄴ)
accessories are often counted with 개/하나
examples: 목도리를 해요.
I wear a scarf.
For neck-wrapped items Korean uses 하다 or 두르다, not 입다.
바람이 차서 목도리를 두르고 나갔어요.
The wind was cold so I wrapped a scarf and went out.
두르다 ('wrap around') paints the wrapping motion more vividly than 하다.
목도리를 목에 한 번 더 둘렀어요.
I wrapped the scarf around my neck one more time.
Real situation: 목에 두르다 spells out the body part; 한 번 더 = 'one more time'.

Because it is draped rather than slipped on, Korean uses 하다 ('do/wear') or, more vividly, 두르다 ('wrap around') — not 입다, 쓰다, or 신다. This is a great example of why English 'wear' cannot map to one Korean verb: the verb here is chosen by HOW the item attaches (wrapping), giving learners a fourth pattern beyond 입다/신다/쓰다/끼다. The pitfall is reaching for 입다 by reflex, or over-using 하다 when 두르다 better captures the action. A thin fashion scarf is more often 스카프, and you might 매다 ('tie') it. Natural collocations: 목도리를 하다/두르다/풀다, 목에 두르다 (wrap round the neck), 따뜻한 목도리, 목도리를 풀다 (unwrap/take off). Note the 'take off' verb here is 풀다 ('undo/loosen'), not 벗다, because you unwind it.

mistakes: Saying 목도리를 입어요 with default 입다. A neck-wrap takes 하다 or 두르다: 목도리를 해요 / 둘러요.
Using 벗다 to remove it (목도리를 벗다). Because it is wound on, you unwind it with 풀다: 목도리를 풀어요.
Treating 목도리 and 스카프 as identical. 목도리 implies a warm winter muffler; a thin decorative scarf is usually 스카프.

usage: 새 is an unchanging prenoun meaning 'new'
어울리다 with the item marked by 이
examples: 안경을 써요.
I wear glasses.
Glasses sit on the face, so the verb is 쓰다 — the very same verb as for a hat.
눈이 나빠서 안경을 써야 해요.
My eyesight is bad so I have to wear glasses.
눈이 나쁘다 ('eyes are bad') is the idiom for poor vision; -아야 하다 = 'have to'.
운전할 때만 안경을 쓰고 평소엔 렌즈를 껴요.
I only wear glasses when driving and usually wear contacts.
Real situation: note contacts (렌즈) take 끼다, while glasses take 쓰다 — different verbs for the eyes.
nuance: 안경 (眼鏡, 眼 'eye' + 鏡 'mirror/lens', literally 'eye-lens') rests on the face, so it takes 쓰다, the same head/face-zone verb used for hats and umbrellas; it never takes 입다 or 신다. A subtle but high-value contrast: glasses 쓰다, but contact lenses 끼다 (the hands/snug-fit verb), because lenses slip directly onto the eye — so the very same 'eyewear' splits across two verbs depending on the object. The core English-speaker pitfall is the single-'wear' habit, compounded by 쓰다 being a heavy homonym (write/use/bitter/wear-on-head). To take glasses off you use 벗다, the universal removal verb. Sunglasses are 선글라스 and also take 쓰다. Natural collocations: 안경을 쓰다/벗다, 안경이 어울리다, 안경을 맞추다 (get glasses made to prescription), 안경을 닦다 (wipe the lenses). Note 맞추다 ('have custom-made/fitted') is the special verb for ordering prescription glasses, distinct from simply 사다.

usage: a wristwatch is fastened on with 차다
멈추다 = to stop; subject marker 가
examples: 시계를 차요.
I wear a watch.
A wristwatch is strapped on, so the verb is 차다 ('fasten on'), not 입다.
약속에 늦을까 봐 자꾸 시계를 봤어요.
I kept checking my watch in case I'd be late.
시계를 보다 = 'check/look at the time'; -ㄹ까 봐 = 'in case/for fear that'.
벽에 걸린 시계가 십 분 빨라요.
The clock on the wall is ten minutes fast.
Real situation: the same word 시계 also means a wall clock, distinguished by 벽에 걸린 ('hung on the wall').
nuance: 시계 (時計, 時 'time' + 計 'measure', literally 'time-measurer') covers both a wristwatch and a wall clock — context tells them apart (손목시계 = wristwatch, 벽시계 = wall clock). A wristwatch is strapped to the body, so Korean uses 차다 ('to fasten/buckle on'), the same verb used for a belt (벨트를 차다); it does NOT take 입다, 쓰다, or 신다 — this is a fifth dressing pattern keyed to 'things you buckle/strap on'. The standout English-speaker pitfall is again 'wear = one verb', plus the watch/clock ambiguity. A second trap: 'check the time' is 시계를 보다 (literally 'look at the watch'), not a verb like 확인하다 in casual speech. To take a watch off you use 풀다 ('undo/unbuckle the strap') or 벗다. Natural collocations: 시계를 차다/풀다, 시계를 보다 (check the time), 시계가 빠르다/느리다 (the clock is fast/slow), 시계가 멈추다 (the clock stops). Note 빠르다/느리다 describe a clock running fast/slow, an idiom that surprises learners.

usage: 편한 is the adnominal of 편하다
examples: 운동화를 신어요.
I wear sneakers.
All footwear takes 신다 — never 입다, even for athletic shoes.
발이 편한 운동화를 신고 많이 걸었어요.
I walked a lot in comfortable sneakers.
발이 편하다 ('feet are comfortable') is the set phrase for comfy shoes.
등산은 안 하지만 운동화가 편해서 자주 신어요.
I don't hike, but sneakers are comfy so I wear them often.
Real situation: 신다 covers habitual wearing too; 자주 신다 = 'wear often'.
nuance: 운동화 (運動靴, 運動 'exercise/movement' + 靴 'shoe', literally 'exercise-shoe') means sneakers/trainers, and like all 신발 (footwear) it takes 신다, the foot-zone verb shared with socks; it never takes 입다. The near-synonym to keep straight is 구두 (dress/leather shoes): both are shoes and both use 신다 and 켤레, but 운동화 is casual/athletic while 구두 is formal — so the choice signals register, not grammar. A pair is counted with 켤레. The English-speaker pitfalls: the single-'wear' habit, and forgetting that the generic word for any shoe is 신발, with 운동화 being one specific type. To take shoes off — a daily act before entering Korean homes — you use 벗다 (신발을 벗다). Natural collocations: 운동화를 신다/벗다, 운동화 한 켤레, 운동화 끈을 묶다 (tie the laces), 운동화가 편하다/낡다 (comfy/worn out). Note 끈을 묶다 ('tie the laces') uses 묶다, and 낡다 ('wear out with age') is the adjective for worn shoes.

mistakes: Saying 운동화를 입어요 with default 입다. Footwear takes 신다: 운동화를 신어요.
Counting with 개 (운동화 한 개). A pair of shoes uses 켤레: 운동화 한 켤레.
Confusing 운동화 with formal shoes. Athletic/casual shoes are 운동화; leather dress shoes are 구두 — both grammar-identical but different in register.

usage: 검은 is the adnominal of 검다 ('black')
examples: 구두를 신어요.
I wear dress shoes.
Formal leather shoes still take 신다, like every other shoe.
발이 아파서 구두를 벗고 슬리퍼로 갈아 신었어요.
My feet hurt so I took off the dress shoes and changed into slippers.
갈아 신다 ('change footwear') is the foot-specific 'change into' verb.
정장에 맞춰 검은 구두를 신고 면접에 갔어요.
I wore black dress shoes to match my suit for the interview.
Real situation: 정장에 맞추다 ('match to a suit') shows 구두's formal register.
nuance: 구두 is the native everyday word for formal leather shoes (often dress/heeled shoes), and like all footwear it takes 신다 and is counted with 켤레; it never takes 입다. The key contrast is with 운동화 (sneakers): grammatically identical — both 신다, both 켤레 — but 구두 carries a formal, dressed-up register (worn with a suit, 정장, to work or interviews) while 운동화 is casual and athletic, so picking the right noun signals the occasion. The broad cover term for any shoe remains 신발. English-speaker pitfalls: the 'wear = one verb' reflex, and assuming 'shoes' is one word — Korean forces you to choose 구두 vs 운동화 vs the generic 신발 by formality. Because Koreans remove shoes indoors, 벗다 (신발/구두를 벗다) is a verb you will use daily, and 갈아 신다 means swapping footwear. Natural collocations: 구두를 신다/벗다, 구두 한 켤레, 구두를 닦다 (polish dress shoes), 구두 굽 (the heel of the shoe). Note 닦다 ('shine/polish') pairs especially with leather 구두, and 굽 is the heel.
